sections.history: Anbil, in Tiruchirappalli district on the bank of the Kollidam near Lalgudi, is the Tiruanbilalanthurai of the Tevaram, one of the Paadal Petra Sthalams sung by Sambandar and Appar, and counted as the 57th Shiva temple on the northern bank of the Kaveri. The oldest parts of the present masonry are Chola work of about the ninth century, and later patrons, among them the Thanjavur Nayaks and Marathas, enlarged the temple, as its many inscriptions record. The village is also known in Chola history for the Anbil plates of Sundara Chola, among the earliest Chola copper-plate grants, and for Aniruddha Brahmarayar, his minister, who is linked in one account with inscriptions of this temple. Sources differ on how closely the plates relate to the Shiva shrine itself.
sections.architecture: The temple faces east beneath a five-tiered gopuram, the tallest feature of its Dravidian skyline. In the east-facing sanctum stands the swayambhu linga of Sathyavageeswarar, and the goddess Soundara Nayaki is honoured as his consort. The courtyard holds shrines to the Saptamatas, Bhikshatanar, Kasi Viswanathar with Visalakshi, Bhairava, Murugan and the nine planetary deities, along with a much-loved Ganesha known as Chevi Saitha Vinayakar, the Vinayaka who inclined his ear. The sacred tree of the temple is the banyan.
sections.legends: The name Sathyavageeswarar, the Lord of true speech, is explained by local tradition through the sage Vageesar, who sought Shiva's blessing here, while Brahma, who came from Satyaloka to worship, gave the Lord his other name, Brahmapureeswarar. The best-loved story belongs to Sambandar. Coming to the Kollidam in flood, the child saint could not cross and sang his hymn from the far bank. Shiva, it is said, had sent the flood to test him, and the temple's Ganesha seemed to lean forward to hear the song more clearly, which is how he came to be called Chevi Saitha Vinayakar. One account adds that the Chola king Paranthaka settled Sama Veda brahmins here to chant before this Vinayaka, giving him the name Sama Veda Vinayakar. These are traditions of the place and are told as such.
sections.festivals: The temple is said to keep five festivals through the year. Among those named in temple listings are Margazhi Tiruvadirai in December or January, Masi Maha Shivaratri in February or March, and Panguni Uthiram in March or April. The monthly Pradosham is observed as at every Shiva temple. Dates follow the Tamil calendar, so confirm them locally.
sections.experience: Anbil makes an easy, unhurried visit. Come in under the five-tiered gopuram, worship Sathyavageeswarar in the sanctum and Soundara Nayaki beside him, then circle the courtyard shrines and pause before Chevi Saitha Vinayakar, whose story is the best way into the place. From the temple it is a short way to the Kollidam, where one can picture the young Sambandar singing across the flood. In the same village stands the Vishnu temple of Sundararaja Perumal, and many pilgrims visit both in one day.

visit.timings: Reported hours are roughly 6:00 to 11:00 in the morning and 5:00 to 8:00 in the evening. Confirm timings locally, especially on festival days.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional attire is expected: dhotis or trousers for men, sarees, salwar kameez, or long skirts for women, with shoulders and knees covered. Footwear is left outside the temple.
visit.photography: Photography is generally permitted in the outer corridors and courtyards but prohibited inside the inner sanctum, in keeping with Tamil Nadu temple rules. Ask temple staff before photographing rituals or priests.
visit.gettingThere: Anbil lies on the bank of the Kollidam, about 8 km east of Lalgudi and some 20 km from Tiruchirappalli, and is reached by road from both. Tiruchirappalli has the nearest major railway junction and airport.
